figure-001.summary: Ancient Greek poet who left the “Iliad” and the “Odyssey,” epics of the Trojan War.
facts: The English word “odyssey,” meaning a long, adventurous journey, comes from his work.
Whether he was really one person or a blend of many poets' songs is still debated.

figure-002.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician whose name is attached to the theorem about the three sides of a right triangle.
facts: The theorem was already in use in Babylon more than a thousand years before him.
He is said to have discovered that a note's pitch is set by the ratio of string lengths.

figure-003.summary: Chinese philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period who taught benevolence and propriety, and whose sayings his disciples compiled into the “Analects.”
facts: At the Confucian shrine of Sungkyunkwan in Korea, the Seokjeon Daeje rite is still held in his honor every spring and fall.
He wandered from state to state for 14 years in search of a ruler who would put his ideas into practice.

figure-004.summary: Ancient Chinese philosopher, traditionally credited with the “Tao Te Ching,” who taught a life free of forced effort.
facts: The “Records of the Grand Historian” tells of Confucius coming to him to ask about rites.
The familiar saying “The highest good is like water” comes from Chapter 8 of the “Tao Te Ching.”

figure-005.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher who asked question after question until others reached the truth for themselves.
facts: He never wrote a single book, so we know him only through his students' accounts.
He drank hemlock in 399 BC, but he never actually said “A bad law is still the law.”

figure-006.summary: Ancient Greek physician who saw disease as a natural process rather than a punishment from the gods.
facts: The oath recited at medical school graduations bears his name, though it's unclear whether he wrote it himself.
“Life is short, art is long” is the opening line of his “Aphorisms,” and by “art” he meant medicine.

figure-007.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher who wrote dialogues starring his teacher Socrates and set out the theory of Forms.
facts: The word “academy,” meaning a school or learned society, comes from the name of the school he founded in Athens.
In the “Republic,” he described a state ruled by philosopher-kings.

figure-008.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher who delved into everything from logic to biology and divided knowledge into distinct fields.
facts: He was a student of Plato and a teacher of Alexander the Great.
He founded the Lyceum, where he collected materials and taught.

figure-009.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician whose “Elements” organized geometry into a single system.
facts: Starting from five postulates, he built up theorems one step at a time.
He is said to have told Ptolemy I, “There is no royal road to geometry.”

figure-010.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician said to have solved the mystery of the king's crown after watching water spill over the side of his bath.
facts: “Eureka,” the cry of sudden discovery, comes from this bathtub story.
He calculated that pi is greater than 223/71 and less than 22/7.

figure-011.summary: Ancient Greek historian who recorded the Persian Wars as he had seen and heard them.
facts: The nine books of his “Histories” were later each named after one of the nine Muses.
Cicero called him the Father of History, yet also chided him for including many made-up stories.

figure-012.summary: Han dynasty historian who saw the “Records of the Grand Historian” through to the end despite being punished with castration.
facts: He perfected the biographical style of history, organized by rulers and individual figures.
Its 130 chapters, totaling over 520,000 characters, cover 2,500 years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu of Han.

figure-013.summary: Ancient Greek astronomer who brought together the geocentric model placing Earth at the center of the universe.
facts: His “Almagest” remained the standard for astronomy for more than a thousand years.
In his “Geography,” he recorded the latitude and longitude of some 8,000 places.

figure-014.summary: Persian physician whose “Canon of Medicine” brought Greek and Islamic medicine together.
facts: The universities of Leuven in Belgium and Montpellier in France used it as a textbook until around 1650.
He also wrote “The Book of Healing,” an encyclopedia of philosophy and science.

figure-015.summary: Medieval Italian philosopher who held that faith and reason do not contradict each other.
facts: His “Summa Theologica” was left unfinished when he laid down his pen in December 1273.
He brought Aristotle's philosophy into medieval Europe.

figure-016.summary: Venetian merchant who traveled all the way to Yuan dynasty China and left the travelogue “The Description of the World.”
facts: He dictated his stories to a writer he met in prison.
Christopher Columbus read the book too and filled its margins with notes.

figure-017.summary: Florentine Italian poet who wrote the “Divine Comedy,” a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise.
facts: By writing in Italian rather than Latin, he laid the roots of the modern Italian language.
Exiled from his native Florence, he died in Ravenna, where his tomb remains.

figure-018.summary: Seventeen-year-old girl who led the French army in the Hundred Years' War.
facts: She relieved the siege of Orléans and led Charles VII to his coronation.
Burned at the stake in 1431, she was canonized 489 years later, in 1920.

figure-019.summary: Mainz craftsman whose metal movable-type printing press made books dramatically cheaper.
facts: In Goryeo-era Korea, the “Jikji” was printed with metal type 78 years before his 42-line Bible.
After losing a lawsuit over debts, he had to hand his print shop over to his partner, Fust.

figure-020.summary: Florentine painter of “The Birth of Venus” and “Primavera.”
facts: Backed by the Medici family, he loved to paint scenes from mythology.
“Botticelli” means “little barrel” and came from his older brother's nickname.

figure-021.summary: Italian Renaissance painter of the “Mona Lisa” who also delved into anatomy and machines.
facts: He filled thousands of notebook pages with mirror writing that can only be read in a mirror.
After his death, the French king bought the “Mona Lisa,” which now hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

figure-022.summary: Nuremberg painter who elevated printmaking into a fine art.
facts: In 1500, at age 28, he painted a self-portrait facing straight ahead, like an image of Christ.
The familiar “Praying Hands” is a drawing he made around 1508.

figure-023.summary: Polish astronomer who moved the center of the heavens with his heliocentric theory that Earth orbits the Sun.
facts: He published “On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres” only just before he died.
The phrase “Copernican revolution,” meaning a complete reversal of thinking, comes from Immanuel Kant comparing his own philosophy to it.

figure-024.summary: Italian sculptor who carved “David” and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
facts: He saw himself as a sculptor rather than a painter and took on the ceiling only reluctantly.
Though he had assistants, he painted most of the ceiling himself over four years.

figure-025.summary: Italian Renaissance painter who created “The School of Athens” and died at just 37.
facts: He was especially renowned for his paintings of the Madonna and Child.
He is buried in the Pantheon in Rome, and his epitaph says Nature feared being outdone by him.

figure-026.summary: Early Joseon painter known for her delicate depictions of insects among grasses and of grapes.
facts: Her portrait has appeared on the 50,000-won note since 2009.
Her son, the scholar Yi I (Yulgok), is on the 5,000-won note, making them a mother and son who both appear on Korean banknotes.

figure-027.summary: Joseon admiral who defended the seas during the Imjin War, leading the way with his turtle ships.
facts: At Myeongnyang, he held off a large fleet with just 13 ships.
He recorded seven years of events in his “War Diary” (“Nanjung Ilgi”).

figure-028.summary: Spanish novelist whose “Don Quixote” portrays an old country gentleman obsessed with tales of chivalry.
facts: He lost the use of his left hand at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, earning the nickname “the one-handed man of Lepanto.”
His face appears on Spain's 10-, 20-, and 50-cent euro coins.

figure-029.summary: Elizabethan English playwright who wrote “Hamlet” and “Romeo and Juliet.”
facts: He left nearly 40 plays and 154 sonnets.
April 23, World Book Day, is the date recorded as the day both he and Miguel de Cervantes died.

figure-030.summary: Italian astronomer who discovered four moons of Jupiter with his telescope.
facts: His experiments on falling objects opened the way to modern physics.
The story that he muttered “And yet it moves” after his 1633 trial by the Inquisition is a later legend.

figure-031.summary: German astronomer who discovered the three laws showing that planets travel in ellipses.
facts: He arrived at his laws by poring over the observations left by his collaborator Brahe.
His novel “Somnium” (“The Dream”), about a journey to the Moon, has earned him a place as a distant ancestor of science fiction.

figure-032.summary: Dutch painter of “The Night Watch,” known for his dramatic use of light and shadow.
facts: He left about 80 self-portraits across paintings, prints, and drawings.
He went bankrupt in 1656 and had to auction off his house and collection.

figure-033.summary: Painter from Delft in the Netherlands who created “Girl with a Pearl Earring.”
facts: Only about 34 paintings are accepted as authentic.
The 2003 film “Girl with a Pearl Earring” imagines the story of the girl in the painting.

figure-034.summary: French philosopher who doubted everything until he arrived at “I think, therefore I am.”
facts: The x-y coordinate plane from math class is called the Cartesian coordinate system after him.
Hired to tutor the Swedish queen at 5 a.m., he died of pneumonia in 1650.

figure-035.summary: English physicist who captured the motion of the heavens and the earth in one framework with universal gravitation and the laws of motion.
facts: He set out the three laws of motion in the “Principia,” and the newton (N), the unit of force, is named after him.
He also showed that a prism splits light into many colors.

figure-036.summary: Venetian composer of the concertos “The Four Seasons,” nicknamed the Red Priest.
facts: He taught music to girls at a school attached to an orphanage.
He wrote some 500 concertos, many of them for the girls at this school.

figure-037.summary: German Baroque composer of the “St. Matthew Passion” and “The Well-Tempered Clavier.”
facts: During his first few years in Leipzig, he wrote a new cantata every week.
He had 20 children, and four of his sons, including Carl Philipp Emanuel, became composers.

figure-038.summary: German-born composer who made his career in England and wrote the oratorio “Messiah.”
facts: Its “Hallelujah” chorus still rings out every year during the holiday season.
He ran his own opera company in London.

figure-039.summary: Engineer who cut the heat loss of the steam engine and sped up the Industrial Revolution.
facts: Adding a separate condenser saved a great deal of fuel.
The watt (W), the unit of power printed on household appliances, is named after him.

figure-040.summary: Austrian composer who shaped the form of the symphony at the court of the Esterházy family.
facts: He wrote 104 symphonies; No. 94 is called the “Surprise” for the sudden loud chord that breaks a quiet passage.
The melody of Germany's current national anthem comes from a song he composed for the emperor in 1797.

figure-041.summary: Swedish biologist who established the system of naming living things with two words, genus and species.
facts: In “Systema Naturae,” he classified plants and animals into groups.
He also gave humans the name Homo sapiens.

figure-042.summary: Swiss mathematician who kept churning out papers even after going blind, leaving more than 800 in all.
facts: He popularized the notation for functions and the symbol for pi.
By solving the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, he founded graph theory.

figure-043.summary: German philosopher whose “Critique of Pure Reason” examined the limits of what humans can know.
facts: His walks were said to be so punctual that neighbors set their clocks by them.
His hometown, which he barely left all his life, is now Kaliningrad in Russia.

figure-044.summary: Austrian composer who was writing music at age five and died at 35.
facts: His operas include “The Magic Flute” and “The Marriage of Figaro.”
He never finished his last work, the “Requiem.”

figure-045.summary: French chemist who launched modern chemistry by showing that burning substances combine with oxygen.
facts: He nailed down the law of conservation of mass through experiments.
Because he had worked for a tax-collecting company, he was sent to the guillotine in 1794.

figure-046.summary: English doctor who developed smallpox vaccination using cowpox.
facts: In Joseon Korea, Ji Seok-yeong learned this cowpox method and gave the first vaccinations in 1879.
The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin word for cow.

figure-047.summary: Swiss educator who took in war orphans and called for nurturing the head, heart, and hand together.
facts: He founded schools for poor children several times.
Froebel, the creator of the kindergarten, also learned from him.

figure-048.summary: Joseon genre painter who captured the daily lives of ordinary people, from ssireum wrestling to village schoolrooms.
facts: As a court painter at the Dohwaseo, he also painted portraits of the king.
Danwon-gu, a district of Ansan in Gyeonggi Province, is named after his pen name, Danwon.

figure-049.summary: German composer who completed his Ninth Symphony after he had become almost completely deaf.
facts: His Fifth Symphony is nicknamed “Fate.”
The melody of the Ninth's final movement became the anthem of the European Union.

figure-050.summary: German mathematician who, as a child, is said to have added up the numbers from 1 to 100 in an instant.
facts: He found how to construct a regular 17-sided polygon with a straightedge and compass.
He calculated the orbit of the lost asteroid Ceres, allowing astronomers to find it again in 1801.

figure-051.summary: German explorer who roamed South America and saw nature as a web of interconnected parts.
facts: He gathered data while traveling up and down the Orinoco River and the Andes.
The ocean current flowing along South America's west coast bears his name.

figure-052.summary: The “King of Song,” who wrote “Erlkönig” and “The Trout” and died at just 31.
facts: He wrote more than 600 songs, and his friends called their gatherings to hear his music Schubertiads.
His Symphony No. 8 stops after two movements and is known as the “Unfinished.”

figure-053.summary: French teacher who lost his sight after injuring his eye at age three and invented a six-dot writing system at 15.
facts: Hunmaeng Jeongeum, the Korean braille created by Park Du-seong in 1926, also follows this six-dot system.
He took his cue from a 12-dot “night writing” system designed for the military but rejected.

figure-054.summary: The 16th president of the United States, who led the Union through the Civil War and proclaimed the emancipation of slaves.
facts: At Gettysburg, he spoke of government “of the people, by the people, for the people.”
In 1865, just five days after the Confederate surrender, he was shot at Ford's Theatre and died.

figure-055.summary: English physicist who discovered electromagnetic induction, producing electricity from magnets.
facts: Starting out as a bookbinder's apprentice, he went on to join the Royal Institution.
He started the Christmas science lectures for children.

figure-056.summary: French inventor who unveiled a photographic process forming images on silver plates in 1839.
facts: Photos taken this way are called daguerreotypes.
He was originally a painter of stage scenery.

figure-057.summary: Danish writer of fairy tales such as “The Little Mermaid” and “The Ugly Duckling.”
facts: Born in Odense as the son of a poor shoemaker, he went to Copenhagen alone at 14.
In 2022, Suzy Lee became the first Korean to win the Hans Christian Andersen Award, named after him.

figure-058.summary: Polish composer who worked in Paris and wrote piano pieces such as nocturnes, mazurkas, and polonaises.
facts: In 2015, Seong-Jin Cho won the Warsaw competition named after him.
After his death, his heart was returned to Warsaw, as he had wished.

figure-059.summary: English biologist whose “On the Origin of Species” explained how living things change through natural selection.
facts: He sailed around the world for five years aboard HMS Beagle.
Mockingbirds that differed from island to island in the Galápagos became a key clue.

figure-060.summary: English novelist whose “Pride and Prejudice” depicts marriage and class among the country gentry.
facts: During her lifetime, she published her books anonymously.
Her portrait appears on the British £10 note.

figure-061.summary: French novelist who wrote “Les Misérables” and “Notre-Dame de Paris.”
facts: For standing up to those in power, he spent 19 years in exile.
More than two million people turned out for his funeral.

figure-062.summary: Russian chemist who arranged the elements in a table by their properties and even predicted the gaps.
facts: Gallium, scandium, and germanium were later discovered and filled the spaces he had left empty.
Element 101 bears his name.

figure-063.summary: Victorian English novelist who wrote “Oliver Twist” and “A Christmas Carol.”
facts: At 12, around the time his father was jailed for debt, he worked in a boot-blacking factory.
Calling a miser a “Scrooge” comes from the main character of “A Christmas Carol.”

figure-064.summary: French chemist whose swan-neck flask experiment disproved the belief that life arises spontaneously.
facts: Pasteurization bears his name, and so does the Korean milk brand Pasteur.
He developed a rabies vaccine and saved a boy who had been bitten.

figure-065.summary: Friar who grew peas in a monastery garden and discovered the laws of heredity.
facts: Over eight years, he observed tens of thousands of pea plants.
During his lifetime, his paper received almost no attention.

figure-066.summary: Swedish inventor who created dynamite and left a will directing that his fortune fund a prize.
facts: He found a way to handle nitroglycerin safely.
The prizes named in his will cover five fields: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace.

figure-067.summary: American author of “The Adventures of Tom Sawyer” and “Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.”
facts: He worked as a riverboat pilot on Mississippi River steamboats.
His pen name came from a boatman's call announcing that the water was two fathoms (about 3.7 meters) deep.

figure-068.summary: Russian writer of “Crime and Punishment” and “The Brothers Karamazov.”
facts: Moments before his execution, his sentence was commuted, and he was exiled to Siberia.
Hounded by debt, he dictated “The Gambler” in less than a month, and the stenographer who took it down later became his wife.

figure-069.summary: Giant of Russian literature who wrote “War and Peace” and “Anna Karenina.”
facts: Born into a family of counts, he set up a school for peasants on his estate.
At 82, he secretly left home and died in the stationmaster's house at the rural Astapovo station.

figure-070.summary: English nurse called “the Lady with the Lamp,” who transformed military field hospitals during the Crimean War.
facts: She charted causes of death in rose-shaped diagrams to push through sanitary reform in military hospitals.
Her birthday, May 12, is International Nurses Day.

figure-071.summary: Italian composer of operas such as “Aida” and “La Traviata.”
facts: Italians still sing the “Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves” almost as a second national anthem.
In his later years, he founded a rest home for poor musicians.

figure-072.summary: British physicist who united electricity and magnetism in a single theory and showed that light is an electromagnetic wave.
facts: He demonstrated the principle behind the world's first color photograph.
He also showed by calculation that Saturn's rings are made of small particles.

figure-073.summary: German Romantic composer who spent more than 20 years refining his First Symphony.
facts: He wrote his “Lullaby” in 1868 when his friend Bertha Faber's second son was born.
He shared a deep, lifelong bond with Robert and Clara Schumann.

figure-074.summary: French painter whose “Impression, Sunrise” gave Impressionism its name.
facts: He painted the same subject again and again as the time of day and the light changed.
He spent his final years painting the water lilies in his garden at Giverny.

figure-075.summary: French sculptor of “The Thinker” and “The Burghers of Calais.”
facts: He worked on “The Gates of Hell” for more than 30 years.
“The Thinker” was originally made as “The Poet,” meant to sit atop “The Gates of Hell.”

figure-076.summary: French painter who painted apples and Mont Sainte-Victoire over and over.
facts: He advised treating nature in terms of the cylinder, the sphere, and the cone.
Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse are said to have called him “the father of us all.”

figure-077.summary: Russian composer of the ballets “Swan Lake” and “The Nutcracker.”
facts: In the “1812 Overture,” he even wrote cannon fire into the score.
For 13 years, he was supported by a patron whom he had agreed never to meet.

figure-078.summary: America's great inventor, who brought the world the incandescent light bulb and the phonograph.
facts: Over his lifetime, he registered 1,093 patents in the United States alone.
The first electric lights in Korea, switched on in 1887 at Geoncheonggung inside Gyeongbokgung Palace, used equipment from Edison's company.

figure-079.summary: French novelist who wrote “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas” and “Around the World in Eighty Days.”
facts: He drew on scientific knowledge to write novels about submarines and voyages to the Moon.
According to UNESCO's count, he is the most translated author after Agatha Christie.

figure-080.summary: Czech nationalist composer who wrote the symphony “From the New World.”
facts: He lived in New York City as director of the National Conservatory of Music of America.
He wove the folk melodies of his homeland into orchestral music.

figure-081.summary: Engineer who patented a three-wheeled automobile powered by a gasoline engine in 1886.
facts: His wife proved the car's practicality by driving it more than 100 kilometers.
The “Benz” in the Mercedes-Benz brand is his surname.

figure-082.summary: Dutch painter of “The Starry Night” and his sunflowers.
facts: In little more than ten years, he produced over 2,000 works.
Hundreds of letters he exchanged with his brother Theo survive.

figure-083.summary: American activist who escaped slavery herself and then led about 70 people to freedom in the North.
facts: She went back to the South about 13 times to bring people out.
During the Civil War, she served as a scout and, in the 1863 Combahee River Raid, helped free more than 700 people.

figure-084.summary: English mathematician who foresaw that machines could do more than crunch numbers.
facts: She wrote out a calculation procedure for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and is called the first programmer.
The programming language Ada, named by the U.S. Department of Defense in 1979, honors her.

figure-085.summary: German physicist who discovered a new kind of ray and named it X because its nature was unknown.
facts: An image of his wife's hand became the first X-ray of the human body.
He received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and never patented the rays.

figure-086.summary: German physicist who proved by experiment that electromagnetic waves really exist.
facts: The unit Hz, used for FM radio frequencies, is named after him.
He died young, at just 36.

figure-087.summary: English surgeon who drastically cut deaths from infection by disinfecting surgical instruments and wounds.
facts: He took his cue for antiseptic surgery from Louis Pasteur's germ theory.
The mouthwash Listerine is named after him.

figure-088.summary: German poet who left us “Faust” and “The Sorrows of Young Werther.”
facts: He worked on “Faust” over a span of 60 years.
The Goethe-Institut, which teaches German, is named after him and has a branch in Seoul.

figure-089.summary: Joseon Silhak scholar who wrote some 500 volumes in exile, including “Mongmin Simseo.”
facts: He designed a lifting crane, the geojunggi, to help build Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon.
Exiled during the Catholic Persecution of 1801, he lived in Gangjin and elsewhere until 1818.

figure-090.summary: Joseon scholar who created the Chusa style of calligraphy and painted “Sehando.”
facts: While in exile on Jeju, he painted “Sehando” for one of his disciples.
By deciphering a stone monument on Bukhansan, he identified it as a border-inspection stele of King Jinheung of Silla.

figure-091.summary: Architect who left Barcelona with flowing, curved buildings that avoid straight lines, such as Park Güell and Casa Milà.
facts: The Sagrada Família is still under construction a century after his death.
In February 2026, its central Tower of Jesus Christ was topped out at 172.5 meters.

figure-092.summary: Austrian painter of “The Kiss,” gleaming with gold leaf.
facts: Turning his back on the established art world, he co-founded the Vienna Secession.
His gold-leaf technique was inspired by the Byzantine mosaics of Ravenna.

figure-093.summary: German physicist who opened the door to quantum theory with the idea that energy comes in discrete packets.
facts: The hypothesis he put forward in 1900 became the starting point of quantum mechanics.
Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined by the value of the constant named after him.

figure-094.summary: Polish-born scientist who discovered polonium and radium and won Nobel Prizes in two different fields.
facts: Together with her husband, Pierre, she coined the term “radioactivity.”
During World War I, she sent mobile X-ray vehicles to the front lines.

figure-095.summary: German-born physicist whose theory of relativity reshaped our understanding of time and space.
facts: He won the Nobel Prize not for relativity but for the photoelectric effect.
He wrote his papers while working as a patent office examiner.

figure-096.summary: Danish physicist who proposed an atomic model in which electrons stay only in fixed orbits.
facts: He founded an institute in Copenhagen that trained young physicists.
He debated quantum mechanics with Albert Einstein for years.

figure-097.summary: Indian mathematician who produced thousands of formulas without ever having formal training in mathematics.
facts: A letter he sent to the British mathematician Hardy led to his going to Cambridge.
He died at 32, and his life became the film “The Man Who Knew Infinity.”

figure-098.summary: British mathematician who worked out a computing machine in theory before one was ever built.
facts: With his colleagues at Bletchley Park, he cracked Germany's Enigma code.
He proposed the Turing test for judging whether a machine can think, and his face appears on the British £50 note.

figure-099.summary: American biologist who discovered genes that jump from place to place in corn.
facts: Her work was so far ahead of its time that it went unrecognized when first presented.
In 1983, some 30 years after her discovery, she won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on her own.

figure-100.summary: British bacteriologist who noticed penicillin in a dish where mold had grown.
facts: Back from vacation, he found that bacteria had died only in the area around the mold.
In 1945, he shared the Nobel Prize with Florey and Chain, who turned penicillin into a drug.

figure-101.summary: Two American inventors who made the first powered flight at Kitty Hawk in 1903.
facts: They built airplanes while running a bicycle shop.
The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 meters.

figure-102.summary: Norwegian explorer who became the first person to reach the South Pole, in 1911.
facts: Using dog sleds was the key to beating his rival.
He was also the first to sail through the Northwest Passage.

figure-103.summary: Soviet cosmonaut who became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1 in 1961.
facts: One orbit around Earth took him 108 minutes.
At liftoff, he shouted “Poyekhali!”—Russian for “Let's go!”

figure-104.summary: American astronaut who became the first person to set foot on the Moon, with Apollo 11 in 1969.
facts: He left behind the words “one small step for a man.”
He had been a Navy pilot and a test pilot.

figure-105.summary: Spanish painter who pioneered Cubism, breaking subjects apart and reassembling them from multiple angles.
facts: With “Guernica,” he exposed the horrors of aerial bombing.
He also painted “Massacre in Korea,” about the Korean War.

figure-106.summary: French painter who led Fauvism, which put intense color front and center.
facts: In his final years, when illness limited him, he worked by cutting out and pasting colored paper.
He originally worked at a law office before turning to painting.

figure-107.summary: Mexican painter who returned again and again to her own face and the pain left by a traffic accident.
facts: A little over a third of her works are self-portraits.
Her life became the 2002 film “Frida,” starring Salma Hayek.

figure-108.summary: Modern Korean painter who drew bulls and children in bold, powerful lines.
facts: Being poor, he even painted on the silver foil from cigarette packs.
In Seogwipo on Jeju, where he stayed as a war refugee in 1951, a street and an art museum bear his name.

figure-109.summary: Italian doctor who created a way of teaching that lets children choose and try things for themselves.
facts: She was one of the first women in Italy to become a physician.
She refined her method at a children’s house she opened in a poor district of Rome.

figure-110.summary: Bengali poet who, with “Gitanjali,” became the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
facts: In 1929 he wrote a short poem for the Dong-A Ilbo comparing Korea to “the lamp of the East.”
He wrote the songs that became the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

figure-111.summary: Writer who skewered old China in “The True Story of Ah Q” and “A Madman’s Diary.”
facts: He was studying medicine when he took up the pen, deciding to heal people through writing instead.
His real name was Zhou Shuren; the name he is known by is a pen name.

figure-112.summary: American author of lean, hard-edged prose who wrote “The Old Man and the Sea.”
facts: He served as an ambulance driver in World War I and as a war correspondent in World War II.
He won both the Nobel Prize in Literature and the Pulitzer Prize.

figure-113.summary: French novelist and pilot who wrote “The Little Prince.”
facts: As an airmail pilot, he flew over the desert and the Andes.
He set out on a reconnaissance flight and never came back, lost over the Mediterranean.

figure-114.summary: Jewish girl who recorded more than two years of life in hiding in a diary she got for her 13th birthday.
facts: Eight people hid in the back rooms of a building in Amsterdam, and only her father survived.
Published by her father in 1947, the diary has since been translated into more than 70 languages.

figure-115.summary: American activist who, unable to see or hear, graduated from college and campaigned for the rights of people with disabilities.
facts: She learned language from her teacher, Anne Sullivan, who spelled words into the palm of her hand.
The dog she was given in Japan in 1937 was the first Akita ever taken overseas.

figure-116.summary: Indian lawyer who fought discrimination in South Africa for 21 years, then came home to lead a nonviolent independence movement.
facts: In 1930 he walked about 390 kilometers in 24 days to protest the salt tax.
His face appears on the front of the Indian rupee notes in use today.

figure-117.summary: American civil rights minister who proclaimed “I have a dream” at the 1963 March on Washington.
facts: The United States honors him with a public holiday on the third Monday of every January.
In 1964, at 35, he became the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate up to that time.

figure-118.summary: American seamstress whose 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat to a white passenger sparked the civil rights movement.
facts: Her arrest set off the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted 381 days.
When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honor in the Capitol Rotunda.

figure-119.summary: Lieutenant general of the Korean Empire’s Righteous Army who shot Itō Hirobumi at Harbin Station in 1909.
facts: He was writing “On Peace in the East” in Lüshun Prison when he was executed in 1910, leaving it unfinished.
Eight months before the shooting, he and eleven comrades cut off their left ring fingers to form the Finger-Cutting Alliance.

figure-120.summary: Sixteen-year-old Ewha Haktang student who led a pro-independence protest at Aunae Market in Cheonan on April 1, 1919.
facts: Both her father and mother were killed by Japanese military police at the protest that day.
She died in Seodaemun Prison in 1920, and in 2019 she became the first woman awarded the first-class Order of Merit for National Foundation.

figure-121.summary: Independence activist who led the Korean Provisional Government and wrote “Baekbeom Ilji.”
facts: He founded the Korean Patriotic Organization and directed the attacks carried out by Lee Bong-chang and Yun Bong-gil.
In 1949 he was shot dead by An Du-hui at Gyeonggyojang.

figure-122.summary: Independence activist who pioneered nationalist history with “The Ancient History of Joseon” and wrote the Heroic Corps’ “Declaration of the Korean Revolution.”
facts: He defined history as “the struggle between the self and the non-self.”
He died for his country in 1936 while imprisoned in Lüshun Prison.

figure-123.summary: King of Macedon who took the throne at 20 and pushed all the way from Greece to India.
facts: He founded about twenty cities named after himself, including Alexandria in Egypt.
He was tutored by Aristotle and died suddenly of illness in Babylon at 32.

figure-124.summary: General who conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon, and became Rome’s most powerful man.
facts: “The die is cast” is said to be what he declared as he led his army across the Rubicon.
The month of July is named after him, and the calendar he reformed was used in Europe for more than 1,600 years.

figure-125.summary: Last pharaoh of Egypt, who allied with two of Rome’s most powerful men to keep her kingdom alive.
facts: Plutarch wrote that she was the first ruler of her dynasty to learn the Egyptian language.
After defeat at the Battle of Actium she took her own life, and Egypt became Roman territory.

figure-126.summary: Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants and marched to the very doorstep of Rome.
facts: At the Battle of Cannae he surrounded and destroyed a Roman army nearly twice the size of his own.
That encirclement tactic is still taught at military academies today.

figure-127.summary: Head of the Library of Alexandria who measured Earth’s circumference using the angle of a stick’s shadow and the distance between two cities.
facts: He put Earth’s circumference at about 250,000 stadia, and he also coined the word “geography.”
A “sieve” for picking out prime numbers is named after him.

figure-128.summary: Teacher of mathematics and astronomy in Alexandria, the earliest female mathematician whose life is well documented.
facts: She edited Book 3 of Ptolemy’s “Almagest” and wrote commentaries on Diophantus.
In 415 she was caught up in a power struggle between the governor and the bishop and was murdered by a Christian mob.

figure-129.summary: Roman physician who learned the inner body by treating gladiators and set the standard for European medicine for over 1,300 years.
facts: Born in Pergamon, in what is now Turkey, he became personal physician to a Roman emperor.
His knowledge came from animal dissection and was often wrong, yet it went largely unchallenged until Andreas Vesalius.

figure-130.summary: Athenian statesman who built the Parthenon and brought democracy to its height.
facts: He paid jurors a daily wage so that even poor citizens could serve in court.
He died of a plague that swept Athens during the war with Sparta.

figure-131.summary: First king of kings of Persia, who united the ancient Near East yet let conquered peoples keep their own faiths.
facts: The Bible says he sent the Jews held captive in Babylon back to their homeland.
A replica of the clay cylinder inscribed with his decree has stood at the United Nations headquarters since 1971.

figure-132.summary: Emperor who united seven rival states into a single realm for the first time.
facts: He standardized the script, weights and measures, and even the width of cart axles.
The pits beside his tomb are believed to hold more than 8,000 life-size figures of the Terracotta Army.

figure-133.summary: Chancellor who came out of retirement after three visits to his thatched cottage and became the pillar of the state of Shu.
facts: From his thatched cottage, he laid out a plan in advance to divide the realm into three.
Legend says dumplings began when he offered sacrifices of dough shaped like human heads instead of real ones.

figure-134.summary: Thinker who held that human nature is inherently good and that the people matter more than the ruler.
facts: He explained innate goodness by saying anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well rushes over in alarm.
The story of his mother moving house three times for his sake is a famous Chinese proverb.

figure-135.summary: General of the state of Wu, traditionally credited with “The Art of War,” which says winning without fighting is best.
facts: The book contains the line “Know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril.”
Drilling the king of Wu’s palace women, he is said to have beheaded the king’s two favorite concubines when they kept laughing.

figure-136.summary: Thinker who preached impartial love for all, friend and foe alike, and traveled around trying to stop wars of aggression.
facts: He and his disciples mastered the art of defending city walls and sided with weak states under attack.
His school once rivaled Confucianism but vanished after the Qin dynasty.

figure-137.summary: Poet of the state of Chu who was banished for his concern for his country and threw himself into a river.
facts: “Li Sao” in the “Chu Ci” is a long ancient Chinese poem of 373 lines and nearly 2,500 characters.
Throwing sticky rice into rivers and racing dragon boats at the Duanwu Festival are said to come from efforts to save him.

figure-138.summary: Tang dynasty poet of wine and the moon, known as the Immortal of Poetry.
facts: He left more than a thousand poems and was famous for composing on the spot.
Legend says he drowned trying to grab the moon’s reflection in a river.

figure-139.summary: Tang dynasty poet who recorded the hardships of ordinary people in wartime and is known as the Sage of Poetry.
facts: “The nation is broken, but mountains and rivers remain” is the opening line of “Spring View,” written in war-torn Chang’an.
In 1481, under King Seongjong of Joseon, his poems were translated into Hangul in “Dusi Eonhae.”

figure-140.summary: Master calligrapher of the Eastern Jin who raised handwriting to an art and is known as the Sage of Calligraphy.
facts: His most famous work is the “Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Poems,” written at a gathering of friends at the Orchid Pavilion.
The original is said to have been buried with Emperor Taizong of Tang, and only copies survive today.

figure-141.summary: General descended from Gaya royalty who led Silla’s unification of the Three Kingdoms.
facts: Raised as a hwarang, he joined King Muyeol and King Munmu in conquering Baekje and then Goguryeo.
He died during the Silla–Tang War and, rare for a subject, was posthumously honored as King Heungmu the Great.

figure-142.summary: Silla man of letters who went to Tang China at 12 and passed the civil service exam there.
facts: Legend says the rebel leader Huang Chao was so shaken reading his “Proclamation Against Huang Chao” that he fell off his seat.
He submitted some ten reform proposals to Queen Jinseong and was promoted to achan, but in the end he withdrew to Haeinsa Temple on Mount Gaya.

figure-143.summary: Founder of the Mongol Empire, who united the tribes of the Mongolian steppe and was proclaimed supreme ruler in 1206.
facts: He organized his army into units of ten, a hundred, and a thousand, and the relay-station network he built spread across the whole empire in his son’s time.
He brought the Uyghur script to the then-unwritten Mongols so their laws could be recorded.

figure-144.summary: Fifth supreme ruler of the Mongols, who founded the Yuan dynasty in China and made Dadu (today’s Beijing) his capital.
facts: He is said to have kept Marco Polo at his court and in his service for many years.
He married his daughter to King Chungnyeol of Goryeo and, drawing on Goryeo troops, invaded Japan twice without success.

figure-145.summary: Tang dynasty monk who crossed the desert alone to India in search of scriptures and made it back.
facts: He returned after 17 years carrying 657 Buddhist texts and spent the rest of his life translating them.
His journey, greatly embellished, became the monk Tang Sanzang in “Journey to the West.”

figure-146.summary: Italian friar born to a rich family who gave up his wealth and chose poverty.
facts: San Francisco took its name from a mission named after him.
Pope Francis, elected in 2013, took his name.

figure-147.summary: Twelfth-century abbess of a convent on the Rhine who wrote down her visions and composed sacred chants.
facts: Sixty-nine of her chants survive, along with the music for a work considered the oldest morality play.
She also wrote two books on medicinal herbs and illnesses.

figure-148.summary: English poet who wrote “The Canterbury Tales,” in which pilgrims take turns telling stories.
facts: He wrote in English rather than Latin, earning the title “father of English literature.”
His characters span every rank of society, from knights to millers.

figure-149.summary: Poet who poured his love for Laura into sonnets and opened the door to the Renaissance.
facts: He hunted down forgotten ancient manuscripts and is called the father of humanism.
The idea of the thousand years after Rome as a “Dark Age” began with him.

figure-150.summary: Author of “The Decameron,” in which ten people fleeing the Black Death at a country villa tell 100 stories over ten days.
facts: He mocked human greed without sparing anyone, clergy and merchants alike.
He was a friend and correspondent of Petrarch.

figure-151.summary: Prague theologian who challenged the Church’s wrongs a century before Martin Luther and was burned at the stake.
facts: He preached in Czech and is believed to have written the spelling treatise that gave rise to the háček (ˇ).
The wars waged by his followers went on for nearly 15 years.

figure-152.summary: Medieval debater who insisted that even faith must be questioned and brought logic into theology.
facts: His letters with his student Héloïse survive as one of the Middle Ages’ most famous love stories.
His method of setting arguments for and against side by side became the basis of university teaching.

figure-153.summary: Goryeo man of letters who stayed with King Chungseon at the Mangwondang library in Yuan China, mingling with Chinese scholars.
facts: He left “Soakbu,” which renders 17 Goryeo folk songs as classical Chinese poems of seven-character quatrains.
His portrait, painted by the Yuan artist Chen Jianru, is designated a National Treasure.

figure-154.summary: Scholar who copied Zhu Xi’s books in Yuan China and first brought Neo-Confucianism to Goryeo.
facts: He set up a scholarship fund called Seomhakjeon to revive the declining national academy.
Sosu Seowon, Korea’s first private Confucian academy, enshrines him and became a World Heritage Site in 2019.

figure-155.summary: Loyal Goryeo official who refused to the end to back a new dynasty and was killed on Seonjuk Bridge.
facts: “Dansimga,” which opens with “Though I die and die again,” is said to have been his reply.
Deeply versed in Neo-Confucianism, he is called the founder of the School of Principle in Korea.

figure-156.summary: Genoese sailor who crossed the Atlantic believing that sailing west would bring him to India.
facts: Backed by the Spanish crown, he set out with three ships and in 1492 reached an island in the West Indies.
He believed until his death that he had reached India, which is why Native Americans are still called Indians.

figure-157.summary: Portuguese sailor who led the first fleet to sail all the way around the world.
facts: After passing through the strait at the tip of South America, he named the calm ocean he found the Pacific.
He himself was killed in battle in the Philippines, and only one ship and 18 men made it home.

figure-158.summary: Florentine navigator who realized the newly found lands were not India but a separate continent.
facts: He spread the news widely in letters, and a mapmaker put his name on the continent.
The name “America” first appeared on Waldseemüller’s 1507 world map.

figure-159.summary: Monk who sparked the Reformation by posting the 95 Theses against a Church that was selling indulgences.
facts: He translated the Bible into German so that anyone could read it.
That translation became the root of today’s standard German.

figure-160.summary: Leader of the second wave of the Reformation, who championed predestination from his base in Geneva.
facts: He systematized Protestant theology in “Institutes of the Christian Religion.”
His teachings spread to the Netherlands, Scotland, and America.

figure-161.summary: Humanist from Rotterdam who poked fun at the Church and scholars alike in “The Praise of Folly.”
facts: His new edition of the New Testament from the Greek original helped light the spark of the Reformation.
Yet he clashed bitterly with Martin Luther over human free will.

figure-162.summary: Lord Chancellor of England who coined the word “Utopia” by describing an island nation that exists nowhere.
facts: On that island people work only six hours a day, and gold is used to make chamber pots.
He refused to recognize the king as head of the English Church and was executed for treason.

figure-163.summary: Florentine official long vilified for advising rulers to protect the state rather than be good.
facts: In “The Prince” he wrote that it is safer to be feared than loved.
He himself supported the republic and wrote his books in the countryside after being forced out of office.

figure-164.summary: Last monarch of the Tudor dynasty, who never married and ushered in England’s golden age.
facts: She defeated the Spanish fleet known as the Invincible Armada.
The U.S. state of Virginia is named after her, the “Virgin Queen.”

figure-165.summary: Anatomist who dissected human bodies himself and corrected the errors of a thousand-year-old medical canon.
facts: The accurate illustrations in “On the Fabric of the Human Body” became the model for later anatomical drawings.
His teachers resented him for contradicting Galen.

figure-166.summary: Italian painter who built form with color rather than line and perfected the Venetian style.
facts: Emperors and popes competed to have him paint their portraits.
He lived to nearly 90 and never put down his brush.

figure-167.summary: Painter from Crete who depicted Toledo with elongated figures and cold, eerie light.
facts: His name is a nickname mixing Spanish and Italian that means “the Greek.”
Dismissed as bizarre in his own day, he was rediscovered 300 years later by the Expressionists.

figure-168.summary: Wandering physician who urged people to learn from miners and barbers instead of old books.
facts: He left the saying “All things are poison, and nothing is without poison; only the dose decides.”
He tried to treat illness with metals and minerals, bringing chemistry into medicine.

figure-169.summary: Former monk and storyteller who mocked the Church and the schools wholesale through the comic adventures of a father and son who were giants.
facts: In 1543 the Sorbonne’s faculty of theology condemned two of his giant books and banned them.
The English word “gargantuan” comes from his giant Gargantua.

figure-170.summary: Author of the “Essays,” who examined himself while asking over and over, “What do I know?”
facts: The essay as a literary form began with this book.
At 38 he gave up public office and shut himself away in the tower of his château to write.

figure-171.summary: Flemish painter who used oil-based paints to capture even the textures of glass and fur.
facts: In “The Arnolfini Portrait,” tiny figures are reflected in a convex mirror.
Above the mirror he wrote “Jan van Eyck was here.”

figure-172.summary: Painter whose hellscapes teeming with monsters, eggs, and musical instruments have remained a riddle for 500 years.
facts: When the panels of “The Garden of Earthly Delights” are closed, a gray globe appears on the outside.
Only about 25 of his paintings survive, and not a single letter.

figure-173.summary: Portrait painter who recorded the faces of the king and his courtiers at the court of Henry VIII.
facts: The distorted smear at the bottom of “The Ambassadors” turns into a skull when viewed from an angle.
Henry VIII married Anne after seeing his portrait of her, and the marriage ended after just six months.

figure-174.summary: Pioneer of Renaissance architecture who raised the huge dome of Florence Cathedral without scaffolding supports.
facts: He laid the bricks in a herringbone pattern so the dome would not collapse.
He also proved through experiment the perspective rule that distant objects look smaller.

figure-175.summary: Preacher who shook Florence for four years, urging people to burn their luxuries.
facts: He staged the “Bonfire of the Vanities,” piling mirrors, paintings, and books in a square and setting them alight.
After defying the pope, he was hanged and burned in that same square.

figure-176.summary: Sultan who led the Ottoman Empire to its height, expanding its lands so far that he besieged Vienna.
facts: In Turkey he is called “Kanuni” (the Lawgiver) for overhauling the law.
He wrote poetry, learned goldsmithing, and left a famous mosque in Istanbul.

figure-177.summary: Chief state councillor who, as supreme commander and prime minister during the Imjin War, managed Ming troops and supplies and steered the country through the crisis.
facts: He was the one who recommended Yi Sun-sin, then magistrate of Jeongeup, as Left Naval Commander of Jeolla.
After the war he wrote “Jingbirok” so that such a disaster would never happen again.

figure-178.summary: French absolute monarch who built the Palace of Versailles and reigned for more than 72 years.
facts: There is no reliable record that he ever actually said “I am the state.”
His role as the sun god Apollo in a 1653 ballet became the basis of his Sun King image.

figure-179.summary: Reforming Russian ruler who traveled to Western Europe in disguise to learn shipbuilding firsthand.
facts: He built a new capital, Saint Petersburg, on marshland.
He taxed nobles’ long beards to push Western-style dress.

figure-180.summary: Puritan general who had the king beheaded and briefly ruled a kingless England.
facts: He built a new cavalry force that crushed the king’s army.
After his death, when the monarchy returned, his body was dug up and executed again.

figure-181.summary: Lens-grinding philosopher who, after being cast out of the Jewish community, argued that God and nature are one and the same.
facts: He wrote the “Ethics” like a geometry textbook, with definitions and proofs.
He turned down a university professorship and made his living grinding lenses.

figure-182.summary: English thinker, called the father of liberalism, who held that the human mind starts out as a blank slate.
facts: He wrote that if a government fails to protect its citizens’ life, liberty, and property, they may replace it.
The “long train of abuses” phrase in the U.S. Declaration of Independence was lifted straight from his “Two Treatises of Government.”

figure-183.summary: Author of “Leviathan,” who called the state of nature “the war of all against all.”
facts: He argued that people make a contract handing all their power to the state in order to end the fighting.
The giant on the book’s cover is made up of many tiny people.

figure-184.summary: German mathematician and philosopher who invented calculus independently of Isaac Newton.
facts: The integral sign and the dx notation we use today are his.
He refined binary notation, writing numbers with 0 and 1, laying the groundwork for modern computing.

figure-185.summary: French mathematician who built a calculating machine at 18 to help his father with tax calculations.
facts: The hectopascal (hPa), the pressure unit heard in weather forecasts, comes from his name.
After he died at 39, his notes were published as “Pensées,” which includes the “thinking reed.”

figure-186.summary: French lawyer who scribbled in a book’s margin that it was too narrow to contain his proof.
facts: That one line kept mathematicians busy for 358 years.
Andrew Wiles finally solved it in 1994.

figure-187.summary: Chemist whose name is attached to the law that a gas’s volume is inversely proportional to its pressure.
facts: Born in Ireland, he carried out experiments with a vacuum pump at Oxford.
He wrote “The Sceptical Chymist,” which separated chemistry from alchemy.

figure-188.summary: Physician who used calculation to prove that blood circulates through the body and returns to where it started.
facts: He calculated that the heart pumps out more blood in half an hour than the body holds in total.
This toppled Galen’s explanation, which had stood for 1,400 years.

figure-189.summary: Court painter who layered mirrors and gazes to pull the viewer into the picture.
facts: “Las Meninas” shows the painter himself and the king and queen in a single scene.
He painted dwarfs and jesters at the same eye level as royalty.

figure-190.summary: Flemish painter who led Baroque art with lush flesh and swirling, dynamic bodies.
facts: He traveled between countries as a diplomatic envoy and was knighted.
The English word “Rubenesque,” meaning plump and full-figured, comes from his name.

figure-191.summary: Painter who cast a single shaft of light into darkness and painted saints like ordinary people from the market.
facts: He used people straight off the street as models, provoking a backlash from the Church.
After killing a man in a brawl, he kept painting while on the run and died at 38.

figure-192.summary: Enlightenment polemicist who wrote “Candide” and attacked Church and king with nothing but his pen.
facts: Even when locked in the Bastille and exiled to England, he never stopped writing.
He spent three years getting the verdict overturned for Calas, a Protestant who had been broken on the wheel.

figure-193.summary: Author of “The Social Contract,” which opens: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.”
facts: Born in Geneva, he wrote in France, and his ideas were taken up by revolutionaries.
“Emile,” which urged raising children as children, was burned as soon as it came out.

figure-194.summary: Bordeaux judge who proposed splitting power into legislative, executive, and judicial branches to check one another.
facts: “The Spirit of the Laws” came out anonymously in 1748 and was banned by the Church three years later.
The separation of powers became the backbone of the U.S. Constitution.

figure-195.summary: Author of “The Wealth of Nations,” who argued that when everyone pursues their own interest, an invisible hand balances the whole.
facts: Using a pin factory as an example, he showed how much the division of labor boosts production.
His face appeared on the British £20 note from 2007 to 2020.

figure-196.summary: American Founding Father who proved lightning is electricity with a key tied to a kite.
facts: He invented the lightning rod, bifocals, and a stove, yet never took out a patent.
His face is on the $100 bill, but he was never president of the United States.

figure-197.summary: Commander who led the War of Independence and became the first president of the United States.
facts: He stepped down after two terms of his own accord, setting the custom of a term limit.
His face is on the $1 bill, and the capital, Washington, D.C., is named after him.

figure-198.summary: Third president of the United States, who drafted the Declaration of Independence.
facts: He bought Louisiana from France, doubling the size of the country.
He founded the University of Virginia and designed its buildings himself.

figure-199.summary: British naval captain who charted the Pacific on three voyages across it.
facts: By feeding his crews fresh vegetables, he lost almost no one to scurvy even on long voyages.
He was killed in a clash with the islanders in Hawaii.

figure-200.summary: Musician-turned-astronomer who discovered Uranus with a telescope he made himself.
facts: Born in Hanover, he moved to England, playing the organ by day and watching the sky by night.
In 1800 he measured that the region beyond the red end of a prism’s spectrum was hotter, discovering infrared light.

figure-201.summary: Anatomist who saw a frog’s leg twitch when touched with metal and proposed the idea of animal electricity.
facts: Alessandro Volta invented the battery while trying to disprove his interpretation.
Mary Shelley said she had read reports of his experiments before writing “Frankenstein.”

figure-202.summary: Inventor of the first battery, a stack of zinc and copper discs separated by cloth soaked in salt water.
facts: The volt (V), the unit of voltage, is named after him.
He demonstrated it in person before Napoleon and was later made a count.

figure-203.summary: Draper who used lenses he made himself to become the first to see microorganisms in a drop of water.
facts: He never attended university and knew no Latin, yet he sent around 560 letters to the Royal Society and others.
He never revealed how he made his lenses.

figure-204.summary: Scholar who saw light as a wave, built the pendulum clock, and revealed the true nature of Saturn’s rings.
facts: In 1655 he discovered Titan, Saturn’s largest moon.
His pendulum clock cut clock error from 15 minutes a day to 15 seconds.

figure-205.summary: English astronomer who used calculation to predict a comet that returns every 75 to 76 years.
facts: He paid out of his own pocket to publish Isaac Newton’s “Principia.”
The comet returned as predicted 16 years after his death.

figure-206.summary: Pioneer of fluid dynamics who showed that pressure drops where a fluid flows faster.
facts: This principle is used to explain why airplane wings generate lift.
When he shared a Paris Academy prize with his father, his father reportedly threw him out of the house.

figure-207.summary: Minister who showed that plants revive air in which a candle has gone out, and who isolated oxygen.
facts: He made the first carbonated water by dissolving carbon dioxide in water.
After his house was burned for his support of the French Revolution, he moved to America.

figure-208.summary: Author of “Gulliver’s Travels,” who used lands of tiny people and giants to mock human folly.
facts: The computing term “endian” comes from his story of a war over which end of an egg to crack.
He served as dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin for more than 30 years.

figure-209.summary: Author of “Robinson Crusoe,” about a man who survived alone on a deserted island for 28 years.
facts: He is said to have drawn on the story of a real sailor who was marooned on a deserted island.
He published his first novel when he was nearly 60.

figure-210.summary: English poet who completed “Paradise Lost” after going blind by dictating it to others.
facts: He told the story of Adam and Eve’s expulsion from Paradise in a poem of more than 10,000 lines.
He also wrote “Areopagitica,” which argued for publishing without censorship.

figure-211.summary: Master of comedy who got laughs by putting hypocrites, misers, and pompous doctors on stage.
facts: “Tartuffe” was barred from the stage for five years because of opposition from the Church.
He collapsed on stage while performing “The Imaginary Invalid” and died that night.

figure-212.summary: Author of “William Tell,” who put characters crying out for freedom on the stage.
facts: His poem “Ode to Joy” became the text of Ludwig van Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, whose melody is the anthem of the European Union.
While at military school, he secretly wrote his first play, “The Robbers.”

figure-213.summary: Twenty-second king of Joseon, who founded the Gyujanggak library and hired talent regardless of social status.
facts: The crane designed by Jeong Yak-yong greatly cut the labor and time needed to build Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon.
He moved the tomb of his father, Crown Prince Sado, to Suwon and visited it thirteen times in eleven years.

figure-214.summary: Joseon official said to have written a novel in Hangul to comfort his mother while in exile in Seoncheon.
facts: “The Cloud Dream of the Nine” uses a single night’s dream to show the emptiness of wealth and glory.
He argued that only writing in the Korean language was true writing.

figure-215.summary: Scholar of the Northern Learning school who argued that the Earth rotates and that China was not the center of the world.
facts: In Beijing he met Western missionaries and saw their astronomical instruments.
He built an armillary sphere at home to observe the stars.

figure-216.summary: Scholar who left a masterpiece of Joseon self-portraiture, facing his own face with every single hair rendered.
facts: He also painted everyday life, such as women gathering greens and men weaving straw sandals.
He was the great-grandson of Yun Seon-do and the maternal great-grandfather of Jeong Yak-yong.

figure-217.summary: Painter and critic who brought Western shading techniques into Joseon landscape painting early on.
facts: He taught the young Kim Hong-do, and Sin Wi also studied painting under him.
He entered government service after 60 and even traveled to China as part of an envoy mission.

figure-218.summary: French conqueror who rose from junior officer on Corsica all the way to emperor.
facts: He placed the crown on his own head, and the civil code he created still underpins the laws of many countries.
After the failed Russian campaign and defeat at Waterloo, he ended his days confined on an island in the Atlantic.

figure-219.summary: Chancellor who drove the unification of Germany, declaring that the nation would be united not by speeches but by iron and blood.
facts: He fought three wars to bind the scattered German states into one.
To head off socialism, he created the world’s first health insurance and pension programs.

figure-220.summary: German thinker who co-wrote with Engels “The Communist Manifesto,” which ends with “Workers of the world, unite!”
facts: He shut himself away in the British Museum Reading Room in London to write “Das Kapital.”
He was poor all his life and got by with help from his friend Engels.

figure-221.summary: Philosopher who declared “God is dead” and spoke of people who create their own values.
facts: He became a professor at 24 but left because of illness, then wandered between mountains and seaside towns writing.
His sister compiled his unpublished notes into “The Will to Power,” and the Nazis later co-opted him.

figure-222.summary: Pessimist philosopher who saw the world as an endless will and the suffering that comes with it.
facts: He brought Indian philosophy into Western thought in earnest.
He scheduled his lectures at the same hour as G. W. F. Hegel’s and was humiliated when only five students showed up.

figure-223.summary: Culminating figure of idealism, who held that the world advances to higher stages through contradiction.
facts: His dialectic was taken up by Karl Marx, who turned it on its head.
He wrote, “The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk.”

figure-224.summary: Liberator who freed six South American nations from Spain.
facts: He crossed the Andes in a surprise attack and liberated Colombia.
The country of Bolivia and Venezuela’s currency, the bolívar, are both named after him.

figure-225.summary: General who led a thousand redshirts and unified Italy starting from the south.
facts: He handed the lands he had won over to the king unconditionally and went back to farming on an island.
In South America, too, he fought for rebels in southern Brazil and for Uruguay.

figure-226.summary: British monarch who reigned for 63 years and whose very name came to stand for an entire era.
facts: The white dress she wore at her 1840 wedding started the fashion for white wedding gowns.
After her husband died, she wore only black for 40 years.

figure-227.summary: British philosopher who insisted that no one's liberty may be restricted unless they harm others.
facts: The popular saying “Better a hungry Socrates than a well-fed pig” comes from a passage in his “Utilitarianism.”
In 1867 he proposed an amendment in the House of Commons to replace the word “man” with “person” in the electoral reform bill.

figure-228.summary: British novelist who wrote “Jane Eyre,” in which an orphaned governess finds her own voice.
facts: To avoid prejudice against women writers, she used the gender-neutral pen name Currer Bell.
In the same year, 1847, her younger sisters Emily and Anne published “Wuthering Heights” and “Agnes Grey.”

figure-229.summary: American poet who, from around age 28, rarely left her house and wrote nearly 1,800 poems.
facts: Only about ten of her poems appeared in print during her lifetime.
After her death, her younger sister found bundles of them in a drawer and shared them with the world.

figure-230.summary: American poet of “Leaves of Grass,” who threw off rhyme and meter to celebrate ordinary people and the body.
facts: He revised the collection all his life, expanding it from 12 poems to nearly 400.
“O Captain! My Captain!” from the film “Dead Poets Society” is his poem mourning the death of Abraham Lincoln.

figure-231.summary: French novelist who linked more than 90 novels into “The Human Comedy,” portraying every class of Parisian society.
facts: He reportedly drank more than 50 cups of black coffee a day while writing through the night.
He made systematic use of recurring characters, bringing figures from earlier works back in later ones.

figure-232.summary: French novelist who labored over a single page for a week at a time and spent five years completing “Madame Bovary.”
facts: The book was put on trial for offending public morals, but was acquitted.
His teaching that there is “only one word” to express any given thing was recorded by his protégé Guy de Maupassant.

figure-233.summary: French writer who exposed human vanity and the seamy side of life in some 300 short stories.
facts: “The Necklace” tells of ten years spent paying off a debt, all because of one fake necklace.
He learned to write from Gustave Flaubert and, at Flaubert's home, mingled with Émile Zola and Ivan Turgenev.

figure-234.summary: French novelist who took the side of Dreyfus, a wrongly accused army officer, in the open letter “J'Accuse…!” (“I Accuse…!”).
facts: In “Germinal,” he depicted a strike by coal miners in northern France.
Convicted of libel over that letter in 1898, he fled to England and lived there for nearly a year.

figure-235.summary: Russian novelist who portrayed the clash between the old and new generations and popularized the word “nihilist.”
facts: Bazarov, the hero of “Fathers and Sons,” became the model for that term.
“A Sportsman's Sketches,” which depicted the lives of serfs, helped build public support for their emancipation.

figure-236.summary: Russian playwright of “The Seagull,” who filled the stage with ordinary daily life rather than dramatic events.
facts: The screenwriting term “Chekhov's gun” comes from his letter advising that a gun no one will fire should never be hung on the stage.
He wrote while working as a doctor and treated poor patients for free.

figure-237.summary: British novelist who pioneered the historical novel, setting his stories among medieval knights and the Highlands of Scotland.
facts: Edinburgh's major rail hub, Waverley Station, is named after the series that began with his first novel, “Waverley.”
When a printing firm he co-owned collapsed in 1826, he was left £130,000 in debt and kept writing until his death.

figure-238.summary: British Romantic poet whose brooding rebel heroes set all of Europe ablaze.
facts: He joined the Greek War of Independence and died of a fever.
Ada Lovelace, often called the first computer programmer, was his daughter.

figure-239.summary: British Romantic poet who longed for the west wind to sweep away the old world.
facts: “If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?” is the closing line of his “Ode to the West Wind.”
He drowned at 29 when his boat capsized off the coast of Italy.

figure-240.summary: British Romantic poet who declared that “Beauty is truth” and died at just 25.
facts: He earned his apothecary's license but gave up medicine to become a poet.
He asked that his gravestone bear not his name but the words “Here lies one whose name was writ in water.”

figure-241.summary: English Lake District poet who reinvented poetry with daffodils in the fields and the plain speech of country people.
facts: The line “The Child is father of the Man” comes from his poem “My Heart Leaps Up,” also known as “The Rainbow.”
“Daffodils” grew out of a scene he saw in 1802 while walking with his sister Dorothy along the shore of Ullswater.

figure-242.summary: British novelist who wrote “Frankenstein” at 18 after a ghost-story contest among friends.
facts: The tale of a science-made being who resents its creator is sometimes called the first science fiction novel.
The monster has no name; Frankenstein is the surname of the man who made it.

figure-243.summary: German composer who wrote “The Ring of the Nibelung,” performed over four nights, and even built his own theater to stage it.
facts: The “Bridal Chorus” played as brides walk down the aisle comes from his opera “Lohengrin.”
After joining the 1849 Dresden uprising, he became a wanted man and fled to Switzerland.

figure-244.summary: Hungarian composer who thrilled Europe by making a single piano sound like an entire orchestra.
facts: Calling a solo concert a “recital” began with his 1840 performances in London.
He taught his students without charging them any fees.

figure-245.summary: German composer who wrote the “Wedding March” heard at weddings and revived the fading music of Johann Sebastian Bach.
facts: He completed the overture to “A Midsummer Night's Dream” at 17.
Several songs by his older sister Fanny were published under his name.

figure-246.summary: German composer who gave up performing after his finger became paralyzed and turned to composing and music criticism.
facts: As a critic, he hailed 21-year-old Frédéric Chopin and 20-year-old Johannes Brahms as geniuses, introducing them to the world.
He even went to court for the right to marry his teacher's daughter.

figure-247.summary: German pianist and composer who first took the stage at nine and kept performing for more than 60 years.
facts: She toured all over Europe while raising eight children.
Before the euro, her portrait appeared on Germany's 100-mark banknote starting in 1989.

figure-248.summary: Italian violinist and composer about whom rumors spread that he had sold his soul to the devil.
facts: He would nick his strings so they snapped mid-performance, then finish the piece on the strings that were left.
The last of his “24 Caprices” was reworked into sets of variations by Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms, and Sergei Rachmaninoff.

figure-249.summary: Italian opera composer who wrote “The Barber of Seville” in less than three weeks.
facts: He gave up opera at 37, and his name lives on in the beef tenderloin dish tournedos Rossini.
His “William Tell” Overture is still used as background music for racing scenes.

figure-250.summary: Italian composer who brought the love stories of ordinary people to the stage in “Madama Butterfly” and “La Bohème.”
facts: “Nessun dorma” (“None shall sleep”) from “Turandot” was the theme of the BBC's coverage of the 1990 World Cup.
He died before finishing “Turandot,” and the composer Franco Alfano completed it.

figure-251.summary: French painter who loved to capture the weary gestures of ballerinas backstage.
facts: He dressed his wax sculpture “Little Dancer Aged Fourteen” in a real tutu and ribbon.
Unlike his fellow painters, he preferred interiors and artificial light to the outdoors.

figure-252.summary: French Impressionist painter who captured people laughing and dancing in the sunlight in warm, glowing colors.
facts: He started out at 13 painting designs on dishes at a porcelain factory.
Even after his hands stiffened, he kept painting with brushes his assistants placed in his grip.

figure-253.summary: French painter who scandalized Paris with “Luncheon on the Grass,” shown at the Salon des Refusés.
facts: He was condemned for painting a nude woman of his own day rather than a figure from mythology.
Young Impressionists looked up to him, yet he never once exhibited at an Impressionist show.

figure-254.summary: French painter who quit his job as a stockbroker and moved to Tahiti to paint in bold, pure colors.
facts: He spent nine weeks with Vincent van Gogh in Arles before a bitter quarrel drove them apart.
The hero of W. Somerset Maugham's novel “The Moon and Sixpence” is modeled on his life.

figure-255.summary: French painter who, instead of mixing colors on the palette, applied them in tiny dots that blend in the viewer's eye.
facts: He spent two years on a single painting, “A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.”
He died at 31 of an illness whose cause remains unclear.

figure-256.summary: Norwegian painter of “The Scream,” in which a figure clutches its face beneath a blood-red sky.
facts: Losing his mother and older sister as a child left a mark on his art for the rest of his life.
“The Scream” exists in four versions, two of which were stolen and later recovered.

figure-257.summary: American dancer known as the mother of modern dance, who cast off pointe shoes and corsets to dance barefoot.
facts: She drew her movements from the poses of ancient Greek sculpture.
In 1927 in Nice, she was killed when the long shawl around her neck caught in the wheel of a car.

figure-258.summary: German physicist, trained as a doctor, who formulated the conservation of energy in its general form.
facts: In 1851 he invented the ophthalmoscope for looking inside the eye and became famous overnight.
He also studied how the ear perceives sound and music.

figure-259.summary: German mathematician whose geometry of curved space laid the mathematical groundwork for relativity ahead of time.
facts: Sixty years later, Albert Einstein adopted that mathematics as it stood.
His conjecture on the distribution of prime numbers is still unsolved, with a $1 million prize on offer.

figure-260.summary: German mathematician who founded set theory and proved that infinity comes in more than one size.
facts: In 1891 he used the diagonal argument to show that there are more real numbers than natural numbers.
Under attack from his opponents, he suffered repeated bouts of depression and died in a sanatorium.

figure-261.summary: French mathematician who showed that the motion of three mutually attracting celestial bodies cannot be solved with a single formula.
facts: This insight became the starting point of chaos theory.
The topology conjecture he left behind was solved about 100 years later, in 2003, by Grigori Perelman.

figure-262.summary: Italian scientist who proposed that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
facts: His name lives on in Avogadro's number, the number of particles in one mole, familiar from high-school chemistry.
Ignored in his lifetime, his idea was accepted only in 1860, four years after his death.

figure-263.summary: German physician who discovered the bacteria behind tuberculosis and cholera, cementing the idea that germs cause disease.
facts: He developed methods for growing one type of bacterium at a time on solid media such as potato slices and gelatin.
World Tuberculosis Day, March 24, marks the day in 1882 when he announced his discovery of the tuberculosis bacterium.

figure-264.summary: French physiologist who showed that the body keeps its internal environment stable even as the outside world changes.
facts: In 1926 the American physiologist Walter Cannon gave this idea the name “homeostasis.”
He was also the first to show that the liver produces sugar.

figure-265.summary: British missionary and explorer who trekked through the interior of Africa, filling in the blank spaces on the map.
facts: The first European to see a vast waterfall there, he named it Victoria Falls after the queen.
After all contact with him was lost, he was found at Ujiji in 1871 by the journalist Henry Morton Stanley.

figure-266.summary: American inventor, originally a painter, who created a telegraph system that sent letters using only dots and dashes.
facts: His name lives on in Morse code, in which the distress signal SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots.
The first telegraph message was “What hath God wrought.”

figure-267.summary: British-born inventor who sent the human voice over wires and received a telephone patent in 1876.
facts: The “bel” in decibel, the unit of loudness, comes from his name.
His mother and his wife were both deaf, and he devoted his life to teaching speech.

figure-268.summary: British engineer who, in 1825, ran a steam locomotive carrying passengers and freight on the first public railway.
facts: He learned to read at 18 and taught himself by working on machines in the coal mines.
The 1,435 mm track gauge he chose became the world's standard gauge, which South Korea's railways also use.

figure-269.summary: British physicist from a brewing family who measured how work turns into heat with an experiment in which falling weights churned water.
facts: The joule (J), the SI unit of energy, is named after him.
Legend has it that even on his honeymoon, he and Lord Kelvin tried to measure the difference in water temperature between the top and bottom of a waterfall.

figure-270.summary: British physicist who devised an absolute temperature scale independent of any substance and calculated its zero to be about −273°C.
facts: He was knighted for helping lay the transatlantic undersea telegraph cable.
The kelvin, the unit behind lighting color temperatures such as 6500K, comes from the noble title he received.

figure-271.summary: French physicist who described in equations the forces by which two current-carrying wires attract and repel each other.
facts: The “A” in the 2A printed on a phone charger stands for the ampere, the unit of electric current named after him.
He named his field “electrodynamics” and also coined the word “solenoid.”
